subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: A variable straight line drawn through the point of intersection of the straight lines x/a + y/b = 1 and x/b + y/a = 1 meets the coordinate axes at A and B. Show that the locus of the midpoint of AB is 2(a + b)xy = ab(x + y).

mark_split.label: Take the variable line in intercept form
Write the midpoint and the intercepts
Put the fixed point on the variable line
Clear the fractions and name the locus

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), chapter 3 THE STRAIGHT LINE, Long Answer question 24, book p.162. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a chapter-level marks banner over this section but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split puts two marks on the fixed point, which is the only piece of the answer that uses the two given lines, two on substituting it into the variable line, and two on the algebra that turns that into the printed locus. Setting up the variable line and naming the midpoint take one mark each, because each is a single line of writing. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q19 to Q21 at 8 marks each, answer any 2 of 3, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The printed folio is hidden or clipped on this scan, so p.162 is inferred from the strictly consecutive neighbours. AUTHOR NOTE on conditions: the card states a ≠ b in its first step (if a = b the two given lines are the SAME line and there is no single point of intersection) and a + b ≠ 0, and it states that the variable line must actually cut both axes, so neither coordinate of the midpoint is zero. None of these is printed in the stem. The result was checked on four concrete positions of the variable line at a = 2, b = 3.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what stays fixed, what varies, and which point you substitute into which line.

steps.label: Find the point of intersection
steps.margin_note: The first two marks. The two given lines are the same equation with a and b swapped, so subtracting them forces x = y and the fixed point falls out in one more line.
lines: Take a ≠ b, so (1) and (2) are different lines.
Then x/a + x/b = 1  ⇒  x(a + b) = ab

recall.must_convey: That subtracting the two given lines gives x = y, so the fixed point is (ab/(a+b), ab/(a+b)).

the fixed point is a b over a plus b in both coordinates
the two lines are symmetric in a and b so x equals y

find where the two given lines meet
heard_as: a b over a plus b

steps.why: Everything in the question varies except this one point, so finding it first is what turns a moving line into a fixed condition.
common_mistakes: Solving the pair by cross-multiplication and losing the symmetry.
Forgetting that a = b would make the two lines identical.
steps.memory_tip: The two given lines are the same equation with a and b swapped, so x = y at their crossing.

steps.label: Take the variable line in intercept form
steps.margin_note: One mark. The variable line is described by where it CUTS THE AXES, so the intercept form is the natural one. Both intercepts must be non-zero for A and B to exist.
lines: Let the variable line meet the axes at
A(α, 0) and B(0, β), with α ≠ 0, β ≠ 0

recall.must_convey: That the variable line is taken as x/α + y/β = 1 with A(α, 0) and B(0, β).

steps.why: The question asks about the midpoint of the two axis points, so the two intercepts are exactly the quantities the answer needs to carry.
common_mistakes: Using y = mx + c, which does not name the two axis points.
Allowing an intercept to be zero, when the line must cut both axes.
steps.memory_tip: The line is described by where it CUTS THE AXES, so use the intercept form.

steps.label: Write the midpoint and the intercepts
steps.margin_note: One mark. Name the midpoint (h, k) and turn it round: the two intercepts are 2h and 2k, so every α and β below can be replaced.
lines: Let M(h, k) be the midpoint of AB

recall.must_convey: That the midpoint is called (h, k) and the intercepts are written as α = 2h, β = 2k.

steps.why: A locus question asks for a relation between the moving point's own coordinates, so the moving point must be NAMED before anything else can be written in terms of it.
common_mistakes: Writing h = α and k = β without the halving.
Using (x, y) for the midpoint too early, which confuses it with the line's own x and y.
steps.memory_tip: Name the moving point (h, k) FIRST, then write everything else in terms of h and k.

steps.label: Put the fixed point on the variable line
steps.margin_note: The next two marks. Every position of the variable line passes through P, so P satisfies (3). Substituting P and then α = 2h, β = 2k gives one relation in h and k.

recall.must_convey: That P is substituted into the variable line and α, β are replaced by 2h, 2k.

steps.why: Passing through P is the ONLY thing every position of the variable line has in common, so it is the condition that produces the locus.
common_mistakes: Substituting the midpoint into the line instead of the fixed point.
Adding the two fractions with denominator hk instead of 2hk.
steps.memory_tip: The one thing every position of the line shares is that it passes through P — that is the condition.

steps.label: Clear the fractions and name the locus
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Cross-multiply, then replace (h, k) by (x, y) because the midpoint is the point whose path is asked for. The check below uses real numbers.
lines: Check a = 2, b = 3, line x/2 + y/3 = 1:

recall.must_convey: That cross-multiplying and renaming (h, k) as (x, y) gives 2(a + b)xy = ab(x + y).

replace h and k by x and y at the end

steps.why: The letters h and k were only a name for the moving point, so the last move is to write the relation in the standard locus letters x and y. Two concrete lines through P confirm it: at a = 2, b = 3 the locus is 10xy = 6(x + y), and the midpoints (1, 3/2) and (3/2, 1) both satisfy it.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer in h and k.
Cancelling hk from both sides, which removes the locus.
steps.memory_tip: h and k were only a NAME for the moving point — rename them x and y at the very end.
